### Part 4: Specific Post-January-2026 Publications

**(a) Measured interventions or failures per operation for an arm in a real SDL campaign.**
The closest publication is Hernández-del-Valle et al. (August 2026, ChemRxiv preprint; DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv.15007960/v1), which reports processing 190 polymer specimens with 2 recoverable errors (1.05%) and 2 undetected errors (1.05%) in a cobot/mobile-robot workflow (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12). However, this reports error rates rather than a standardized human-intervention rate per operation. Moran et al. (May 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s44182-026-00094-z) note that intervention between campaigns appears universal but provide no quantified rates (moran2026theriseof pages 9-11). **No SDL has published a standardized interventions-per-operation metric as of late 2026.**

**(b) Independent accuracy or repeatability characterization of the AgileX PiPER or another sub-$5k 6-DOF arm.**
Zhang (2026; DOI: 10.32920/32253717) integrated the AgileX PiPER in an NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulation framework with AprilTag detection and MoveIt2, validating autonomous pick-and-place in simulation but not reporting physical accuracy or repeatability measurements. Anjaria et al. (February 2026, preprint; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2602.11150) selected the PiPER for YOR at US$2,500 per arm, 4.2 kg weight, but provided no ISO 9283-style characterization (anjaria2026yoryourown pages 5-8). OpenEAI-Platform (Zhang et al. 2026, preprint; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2606.03392) benchmarked the PiPER on manipulation tasks, finding average success rates of 0.64 across four tasks, with failures "concentrated in grasp initiation and precise placement" attributed to its "distinct kinematic and actuation design" (zhang2026openeaiplatformanopensource pages 8-9). **No peer-reviewed independent accuracy/repeatability characterization of the PiPER or comparable sub-$5k arm exists as of late 2026.** Harazono et al. (2024 preprint; DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685) provide the closest methodology—a dial-gauge-based repeatability platform for a low-cost arm—but tested a different robot (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 11-15).

**(c) Vision-corrected manipulation primitives compared open-loop versus corrected on labware.**
Fontenot et al. (2026; DOI: 10.1039/d5dd00541h, peer-reviewed) demonstrated closed-loop vision-corrected manipulation of transparent glass substrates with deep-learning error detection, achieving 98.5% first-attempt success (128/130) and 100% after automatic correction. The system used a 5-DOF xArm with 0.1 mm stated repeatability, fused geometric and CNN models with 97–100% classification confidence, and automatically corrected all 10 pre-programmed failures on the second attempt (fontenot2026closedlooproboticmanipulation pages 1-3, fontenot2026closedlooproboticmanipulation pages 8-10, fontenot2026closedlooproboticmanipulation pages 10-12, fontenot2026closedlooproboticmanipulation pages 3-4). However, the paper does not report a separate open-loop baseline; instead it characterizes the closed-loop system's performance. LIRA (Zhou et al. 2025; DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1) achieved localization accuracy from 0.92 mm (cube-based calibration) to 1.51 mm (filtered ArUco) and 97.5% inspection success across 200 test cases, but likewise did not provide a controlled open-loop comparison (cooper2025liralocalizationinspection pages 3-6). **A direct, controlled open-loop vs. vision-corrected comparison on standard labware has not been published.**

**(d) Arm loading and unloading 3D printers or powder-processing equipment inside a closed experimental loop.**
**No published evidence was found.** Hernández-del-Valle et al. (2026 preprint) demonstrated cobot load/unload of an injection molder within a polymer SDL, involving "8 load/unload operations by the robot arms" (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12), but this was for injection molding, not 3D printing. Dezaki et al. (2026 preprint; DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv.15010111/v1) demonstrated autonomous robotic loading of a furnace at 1600°C for solid-state synthesis, but this involved a furnace rather than a 3D printer. No publication demonstrates an arm autonomously loading build plates into or removing parts from a 3D printer (e.g., Bambu Lab, Prusa) or powder-processing equipment (e.g., ball mill, sieve, gas atomizer) as part of a closed experimental loop.

**(e) Remote users supervising or teleoperating a laboratory arm over the internet, with measured outcomes.**
Hamm et al. (2024; DOI: 10.1002/aisy.202300566, peer-reviewed) demonstrated remote operation of a modular robotic platform for cell culture, with experiments "successfully performed on the robot platform located in Seoul, Korea, by users in Paris, France" and educational remote experiments from Yogyakarta, Indonesia (hamm2024amodularrobotic pages 7-8). The automated transduction process produced significantly more infected cells than manual operation (p = 0.038) (hamm2024amodularrobotic pages 8-9). Robot positioning repeatability was 0.02 mm, and TCP/IP communication was used for control (hamm2024amodularrobotic pages 10-10). However, no remote-specific quantitative metrics (latency, task completion rate, error rate, throughput comparison) were reported. Burger et al. (2020) established remote error reset via CCTV as a practical capability (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 6-12). LIRA (Zhou et al. 2025) supports "remote vision inspection and seamless multi-platform communication" (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 8-9). **No publication reports quantitative measured outcomes specifically attributable to remote (vs. local) supervision or teleoperation of a laboratory arm, such as remote-specific success rates, latency impacts, or intervention frequencies.**

### Summary of Key Gaps for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab

The most actionable and feasible contributions from a lab with a sub-$5k AgileX PiPER arm, Raspberry Pi cameras, 3D-printed fixtures, and remote users would be:

1. **Publish standardized intervention and failure metrics** for real SDL campaigns (interventions per operation, per hour, per experiment)—this is the single most-cited gap across the literature and requires only systematic logging.

2. **Conduct an independent ISO 9283-style accuracy and repeatability characterization** of the AgileX PiPER using cameras or dial gauges—no such characterization exists in the peer-reviewed literature.

3. **Perform a controlled open-loop vs. vision-corrected comparison** for pick-and-place of labware (vials, crucibles, SEM stubs) using AprilTags and Pi cameras on the PiPER arm.

4. **Demonstrate arm loading/unloading of Bambu Lab 3D printers** and powder-processing equipment in a closed design-print-test loop—this has not been published for any 3D printer.

5. **Report measured outcomes for remote users** running experiments via web interface, including task success rates, latency, and intervention frequency compared with local operation.

These gaps are well-aligned with the lab's existing hardware and workflows (aluminium-alloy design, tensegrity structures, gas atomization, powder characterization) and represent contributions that the broader SDL community has explicitly called for but not yet delivered.

| Paper | Limitation category | Key quote or evidence-based summary |
|---|---|---|
| Burger et al. 2020; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2 | Reliability/Uptime; Throughput; Remote oversight; Calibration | GC analysis was the bottleneck; the robot was charged but idle for about 32% of the campaign. Operators received alerts for depleted consumables and failures, and most errors could be reset remotely under CCTV. The eight-day campaign included 688 experiments and 319 robot moves, but no manipulation-failure denominator was reported. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) |
| Dai et al. 2024; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7 | Reliability/Uptime; Integration; Cost | Connecting many modules requires each module to have a very low failure rate. The workflow required more than a year of development and debugging before stable operation. Distributed workflows are proposed, but no per-operation reliability or uptime statistic was reported. (pqac-00000008) |
| Lunt et al. 2024; DOI: 10.1039/D3SC06206F | Solid handling; Reliability; Multi-station integration | End-to-end PXRD automation is difficult because it requires powder handling and sample preparation. The response was a predefined 12-step, three-robot workflow; later assessment notes that such systems still generally need human intervention when logic changes or failures occur. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028) |
| Szymanski et al. 2023; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-023-06734-w | Reliability/Uptime; Recovery; Human oversight | A-Lab ran for 17 days, but manual cleaning, replenishment, and hardware-exception handling remained necessary. Human regrinding and higher-temperature treatment produced two additional targets; no arm-operation failure or intervention rate was published. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030) |
| Zhou et al. 2025, LIRA; DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1 | Perception/Calibration; Error detection/recovery; Scheduling | LIRA addresses the limitation that SDL manipulation is generally open loop. Inspection reached 97.9% across two workflows, but similar colors and clutter caused errors, and recovery still used hard-coded interpretation logic. Future work includes retrying, reordering, replanning, centralized scheduling, multi-view cameras, and image-to-action models. (pqac-00000013) |
| Darvish et al. 2025, ORGANA; DOI: 10.1016/j.matt.2024.10.015 | Perception; Recovery; Scheduling; Oversight; Safety | Robust model-free perception of transparent, reflective, textureless objects remains unresolved. PDDL construction is burdensome, and joint planning and scheduling add overhead. Users favored keeping humans in the loop; half were uncertain about fully autonomous end-to-end operation. (pqac-00000006) |
| Darvish et al. 2025, MATTERIX; DOI: 10.1038/s43588-025-00924-4 | Recovery; Reliability; Safety; Integration | MATTERIX uses a digital twin for precondition checks, collision-free planning, and debugging, but its chemistry model is only semi-quantitative. Future work requires system-specific kinetics and quantum-chemical simulation. Gripper failures, interventions, and campaign uptime were not quantified. (pqac-00000027) |
| Jiang et al. 2023; DOI: 10.1039/D3DD00075C | Grippers/Tools; Perception; Recovery; Throughput; Cost | Dispensing was slow and difficult for compressible, hygroscopic, or deliquescent powders; the demonstrated tools could not dispense sub-milligram quantities. Future work includes self-learning policies, visual feedback, alternative cartridges, capping and decapping, and mobile-robot transfer. (pqac-00000031) |
| Yoshikawa et al. 2023; DOI: 10.1007/s10514-023-10136-2 | Manipulation; Perception; Recovery; Safety | Reliably executing valid plans in the physical world remains challenging. Constrained task-and-motion planning addresses syntax, collisions, and spills, but does not itself provide online detection and recovery from unexpected physical failures. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000028) |
| Zwirnmann et al. 2023; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2302.03644 | Grippers; Cost; Reliability | The compliant fingers cost about €3 each and handled diverse containers, but comprehensive dimensional optimization was outside scope. Future work includes scaling and miniaturization. Testing omitted some vessels, used 2 mm-accuracy displacement measurements, and could not benchmark a Petri dish. (pqac-00000036) |
| Fakhruldeen et al. 2022, ARChemist; DOI: 10.1109/ICRA46639.2022.9811996 | Integration; Scheduling; Cost; Reliability | The motivating limitation is that laboratory robots are commonly programmed for one experiment and depend on proprietary architectures or unconventional hardware. ARChemist provides reconfigurable integration, but later work still finds substantial case-specific tuning and human recovery. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000032) |
| Maffettone et al. 2023; DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2304.11120 | Grippers; Integration; Reliability; Throughput; Cost | Universal human-like grippers remain impractical. Near-term directions are 3D-printed adaptations, tool changers, vessel-specific fingers, and robot-friendly pipettes. Scaling also requires modular hardware, open software, standard interfaces, distributed orchestration, and lifecycle-cost analysis. (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035) |
| Harazono et al. 2024, preprint; DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685 | Grippers; Calibration; Reliability; Cost | Commercial grippers lacked sufficient width, requiring 3D-printed fingers. Repeatability was direction dependent, and lid-placement performance deteriorated sharply beyond a 2.190 mm y-axis offset. No vision correction, autonomous recovery, or campaign uptime was reported. (pqac-00000024) |
| Seifrid et al. 2022; DOI: 10.1021/acs.accounts.2c00220 | Manipulation; Calibration; Recovery; Oversight | Human-like dexterity and hand-eye coordination remain difficult. Solid dispensing below about 20 mg may require material-specific calibration, while heterogeneous mixtures risk blockage and leaks. Proposed work includes robotic arms, continuous vision monitoring, early failure detection, and robot-friendly hardware. (pqac-00000025) |
| Sasaki et al. 2025; DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00492-w | Calibration; Recovery; Reliability; Scheduling | The system reproduces demonstrations but does not adapt when objects or equipment move; task changes can require complete reteaching. Proposed work includes vision-based localization, tactile and force sensing, compliance, positional correction, action segmentation, partial reteaching, and coordinated multi-agent workflows. (pqac-00000000) |
| Salazar-Villacis and Benyahia 2026, ADePT; DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-01932-9 | Grippers; Perception; Recovery; Reliability; Safety | Fine motor control, delicate labware, unfamiliar configurations, autonomous recovery, and real-time replanning remain unresolved. Future work calls for adaptive grippers, tactile and force feedback, richer datasets, stress testing, digital twins, standardized error and recovery reporting, and auditable command standards. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000011) |

info.query:
Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab). Our manipulation hardware is an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, 0.1 mm claimed repeatability, no certified safety functions), SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200) for teleoperation and LeRobot-style imitation learning, Raspberry Pi 5 computers with Pi HQ and Camera Module 3 cameras (wrist-mounted and fixed), AprilTags, a relay-switched arm supply behind a hardwired E-stop, Bambu Lab 3D printers, an Opentrons OT-2, an in-house powder doser, and remote users who run experiments without being in the room. Our self-driving-lab (SDL) work includes AI-guided aluminium-alloy design for laser powder bed fusion (gas atomization, powder characterization, crucibles, SEM stubs) and closed-loop design-print-test of 3D-printed tensegrity structures. Earlier literature scans (September and November 2026) already covered which deployed SDLs use arms (KUKA KMR iiwa, ABB YuMi, Franka, UR, Denso COBOTTA), station recalibration with cubes and ArUco/AprilTag markers (Burger et al. 2020; Zhou et al. 2025, LIRA), ISO 9283 testing with cameras (Chajon et al. 2026), low-cost arms in labs (Rupp et al. 2022; Harazono et al. 2024; Wattoo et al. 2024, RABIT), VLA and imitation-learning success rates and demonstration counts, LabRobFail, MATTERIX, and safety standards. Please do not re-survey those; use them only as starting points.

Question. Mine the stated limitations and future work of the arm-based SDL and laboratory-manipulation literature, and check what has happened since.
(1) For the central papers, including Burger et al. 2020 (Nature, mobile robotic chemist); Dai et al. 2024 (Nature, mobile robots for exploratory synthetic chemistry); Lunt et al. 2024 (modular multi-robot solid-state workflow with PXRD); Szymanski et al. 2023 (A-Lab); MacLeod et al. 2020 and 2022 (Ada); Zhou et al. 2025 (LIRA); Darvish et al. (ORGANA and MATTERIX); Jiang et al. 2023 (dual-arm solid dispensing); Nakajima et al. (robotic powder grinding); Fakhruldeen et al. 2022 (ARChemist); Yoshikawa et al. 2023 (constrained task and motion planning for chemistry); Zwirnmann et al. 2023 (printed compliant fingers for lab automation); Ha et al. 2020 (Fit2Form); Wattoo et al. 2024 (RABIT); Harazono et al. 2024; and any other paper you find central: quote the sentences in which the authors state limitations or future work concerning the manipulation layer, namely grasping and grippers, perception and calibration, error detection and recovery, reliability and uptime reporting, throughput, multi-station integration and scheduling, human oversight and remote operation, safety, and cost.
(2) For each stated item, which later papers (2023 to 2026, preprints flagged) report doing it, and with what measured result (success rate with trial count, accuracy, uptime, intervention rate)?
(3) Which stated future-work items are still unaddressed as of late 2026? Rank them by how often they recur across papers and by feasibility for a lab with a sub-$5k arm, Raspberry Pi cameras, 3D-printed fixtures and remote users.
(4) Separately: since January 2026, has anyone published (a) measured interventions or failures per operation for an arm in a real SDL campaign, (b) an independent accuracy or repeatability characterization of the AgileX PiPER or another sub-$5k 6-DOF arm, (c) vision-corrected manipulation primitives compared open-loop versus corrected on labware, (d) an arm loading and unloading 3D printers or powder-processing equipment inside a closed experimental loop, or (e) remote users supervising or teleoperating a laboratory arm over the internet, with measured outcomes?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints. For each claim give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
